unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 2 pairs an information text on the science of sport and health with the environmental story 'When the Leaves Stop Speaking', in which a young researcher named Amal fights to protect a drying forest. Learners study twenty-eight precise words such as ecosystem, transpiration, efficient, propaganda and restoration, and they master the First Conditional, including 'unless' and modal verbs. They separate fact from opinion, then write a biography, a sports commentary and persuasive pieces of their own.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and the twenty-eight words. Read the sports-science text and the three parts of the story, answering the comprehension questions with evidence. Work through the six grammar sections on the First Conditional, 'unless' and modal verbs. Complete the six activities, then draft and revise the writing tasks. Record the speaking tasks, and finish with the quiz and self-assessment.
unit.origin: Authored Grade 6 source + curriculum review (religion-neutral rebuild)

visual.alt: Illustrated learners linking sport, health and caring for a green forest

readings.title: Training Champions: The Science Behind Sport
readings.setting: East African highlands and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
In many communities across East Africa and around the world, sport has always been more than a game. From the long-distance runners of the highlands to busy basketball courts and football pitches, physical activity brings people together and keeps them strong. But have you ever wondered what happens inside your body when you exercise? The answer involves fascinating biological processes that scientists still study today.
When you run, swim or play football, your muscles need more energy, so your heart beats faster to pump blood around your body. This blood carries oxygen to your muscles so they can keep working. If you train regularly, your heart will become stronger and more efficient. It will pump more blood with each beat, which means it does not have to work as hard while you rest. This is why trained athletes often have lower resting heart rates than people who never exercise.
Nutrition matters too. If you eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruit, vegetables and whole grains, your body will have the fuel it needs to perform well. Protein from foods such as beans, lentils, eggs and fish helps your muscles repair and grow after exercise. If you do not eat enough healthy food, your performance will deteriorate over time. Harmful bacteria can enter your body through unclean food or water, so good hygiene is an important part of staying healthy.
Water is just as important as food. When you exercise, your body loses water through sweat, and if you do not drink enough, you may feel tired, dizzy or unwell. The environmental conditions matter as well: if the weather is very hot, athletes must take extra care to stay cool and avoid heat exhaustion.
Sleep is another vital part of any athlete's routine. During sleep the body repairs itself, muscles rebuild, and the brain sorts through everything it has learned during the day. If a young athlete does not get enough sleep, their reaction times will slow and their concentration will suffer. Most experts say children need between nine and eleven hours of sleep each night.
East Africa's high, cool highlands have produced many of the world's greatest long-distance runners, such as Mo Farah and Tegla Loroupe. These champions did not succeed by talent alone. They trained with discipline, ate well, rested properly and listened to their coaches. Across history, many different cultures have prized physical skills like swimming, running, riding and archery, treating a healthy body as something to value and protect.
Sport also teaches life skills. If you play in a team, you will learn to cooperate, communicate clearly and handle both victory and defeat with grace. In a multicultural society, sport is one of the most powerful ways to bring different people together. Remember this: if you take care of your body today, it will take care of you tomorrow.

readings.title: Reading Closely: Fact and Opinion in Health Writing
readings.passageScript:
Good writing about health mixes two kinds of statements: facts and opinions. A fact is something that can be checked and proven, such as, 'Children need between nine and eleven hours of sleep each night.' An opinion is what someone thinks or feels, such as, 'Football is the best sport in the world.' Skilled readers learn to tell these two kinds of statement apart, because it helps them judge whether a text is fair.
Think about food. It is a fact that protein helps muscles repair after exercise, because scientists have measured it many times. It is only an opinion that beans taste better than eggs, because taste is personal. Both sentences might appear in the same article, so you must read carefully. If you notice words like 'best', 'worst', 'should' or 'I think', the sentence is often an opinion. If a sentence gives a number, a measurement or a result you could test, it is usually a fact.
Water gives us more examples. Scientists have observed that the body loses water through sweat during exercise; that is a fact. If you do not drink enough, you may feel dizzy, and that too can be tested. But, 'everyone should carry a water bottle to school' is an opinion, even though it is sensible advice. Rest works the same way. During sleep the body releases growth hormones and rebuilds muscle, and those are biological facts. Yet, 'staying up late is more fun than sleeping' is only an opinion.
Advertisements sometimes blur the line on purpose. A company may use propaganda, sharing only the facts that make its product look good while hiding the rest. If you read with a careful, questioning mind, you will spot the difference and make wiser choices. Good health writing respects its readers: it separates what is proven from what is merely believed, and it lets each reader decide for themselves.

readings.setting: A future East African research village beside a protected forest
readings.passageScript:
In the year 2083, in the green hills of what had once been northern Uganda, stood a protected grove named Nguvu Wa Asili, which means 'Power of Nature'. Around it lay a self-sustaining, multicultural research village where scientists, farmers, historians and community elders lived and worked together.
Amal, aged twelve, lived in the village. Her parents were both researchers at the local environmental agency, studying soil restoration and the water cycle. Amal loved science, but she also loved listening to the old stories her grandfather told.
'Did you know,' her grandfather would say, 'that long ago a traveller stood under that giant fig tree and promised that light would return after the world's sky broke?'
Amal grinned. 'You mean the supernova of 2081?'
'To me it was a promise; to you it is physics,' he smiled. 'But do not laugh. Some truths are shared in more than one language.'
That year the village was visited by a small agency of international scientists studying transpiration in old forests. 'The plants here release water at incredible rates,' said Doctor Alina, a biologist. 'It may be why the surrounding farmland stays so fertile.'
The villagers had always cared for the grove. Children were taught not to break branches, farmers planted food only at the edges, and elders and herbalists held monthly gatherings at the fig tree to thank the land for its rain. It was a place of peace.
But something was wrong. The outer ring of trees had begun to dry out.
'If the forest continues to deteriorate, the whole ecosystem will collapse,' warned Doctor Alina.
'What is causing it?' asked Amal.
'We are not sure yet,' she said. 'It may involve radiation leaking from a forgotten machine buried during the old wars. Or it could be a bacterial plague.'
Amal had questions. She asked her parents, she asked the scientists, and she even asked her grandfather. He stroked his beard. 'If the ground grows weak, perhaps it is because we stopped listening to it.'
'That is not science,' Amal said gently.
'It is a way of seeing,' he replied. 'And both ways matter.'
The scientists began testing the soil. Amal watched them gather tools and check the leaves for bacteria and radioactive particles. One sample glowed faintly blue. 'It is not dangerous in small amounts,' said Doctor Alina, 'but we should take it seriously.'

readings.title: When the Leaves Stop Speaking, part 2
readings.setting: A future East African research village beside a protected forest
readings.passageScript:
In the village square, meetings were held. A few leaders believed the outsiders were spreading propaganda, spreading fear so that they could seize control of the forest.
'This grove was originally ours to protect,' said one elder. 'Now it is filled with machines and measuring sticks!'
'It must be protected,' argued Amal's mother. 'If we lose it, we lose more than trees. We lose rainfall, clean air, even the ozone above us.'
'If pollution increases,' another scientist added, 'the ozone will keep breaking down.'
Amal began writing her own report. 'The forest,' she wrote, 'is both memory and machine. We must protect it. If we do nothing, its silence will grow loud.'
She collected data. She learned that transpiration had slowed in a quarter of the trees. Some leaves had changed texture, becoming dry and rough. Bark had peeled into strange shapes, like sculpture from a forgotten gallery.
'The change is not only chemical,' she told her mother. 'It feels personal.'
Her mother nodded. 'Sometimes places are like people. When they suffer, they give signs.'
'I want to make people care,' Amal later told Doctor Alina.
'Then make them see,' she replied. 'Use your imagination. Describe what will happen if this forest dies.'
Amal drew posters. One showed a mollusk dying beside a cracked streambed. Another showed the Earth wrapped in smog, a shrinking ecosystem floating like a translucent bubble in space. She built a display titled, 'If the leaves stop speaking, who will listen?'
At the youth assembly the following week, Amal gave a presentation. 'This forest is not just science,' she began. 'It is not just an old story. It is a library, a home and a memory.' She showed graphs, read her predictions and described the forest's architecture: its layers, patterns and hidden connections. 'You must not ignore the evidence. If we act now, we can save it.'
One student asked, 'What if the cause is unknown?'
'Then we keep learning,' Amal said. 'And we act where we can.'
A local carpenter had helped her build a model of the forest's root system, painted with hopeful words in several languages. 'Multicultural does not just mean people,' she explained. 'It means ideas, different ways of seeing, like science and tradition working together.'
The mayor was moved. 'Children,' he said, 'have reminded us of what we forgot. This forest is not ours to own; it is ours to tend.' The council agreed to ban further clearing near the grove. New funding went to clean-up crews and to careful radiation containment, and the agency announced a training programme for local youth.

readings.title: When the Leaves Stop Speaking, part 3
readings.setting: A future East African research village beside a protected forest
readings.passageScript:
That evening, Amal stood at the base of the fig tree again. The wind stirred the top branches gently.
Doctor Alina found her there. 'You have done more than observe,' she said. 'You have inspired people.'
Amal smiled. 'I only followed the data.'
'No,' her grandfather said, stepping out of the shadows. 'You followed your vision.'
Amal looked up at the tree that had watched over so many lifetimes. She thought about the restoration work that would begin in the morning, and about the renewable hope her display had promised.
'Some call it an old story,' she whispered. 'Some call it biology. Either way, it begins with belief, and with the choice to act.'
And the forest rustled softly in return, as if, at last, it had been heard.

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what happens to your heart if you train regularly?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It becomes stronger and more efficient, pumping more blood with each beat, so it works less hard at rest.
comprehension.explanation: The text states that regular training makes the heart stronger and more efficient.

comprehension.question: Name two foods the passage lists that provide protein to help muscles repair.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Any two of these: beans, lentils, eggs or fish.
comprehension.explanation: The passage names beans, lentils, eggs and fish as sources of protein.

comprehension.question: The writer ends by saying, 'if you take care of your body today, it will take care of you tomorrow.' Is this a fact or an opinion, and how can you tell?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is an opinion, because it is a belief about the future that cannot be measured or proven.
comprehension.explanation: This closing line expresses a view rather than a testable, measurable fact.

comprehension.question: How does the passage say you can often recognise an opinion in health writing?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Opinions often use words like 'best', 'worst', 'should' or 'I think'.
comprehension.explanation: The text lists these signal words as clues that a statement is an opinion.

comprehension.question: Give one example from the passage of a fact about water and the body.
comprehension.correctAnswer: The body loses water through sweat during exercise, and drinking too little can make you feel dizzy.
comprehension.explanation: The passage gives these as tested, measurable facts about water.

comprehension.question: Why might a company use propaganda in an advertisement?
comprehension.correctAnswer: To share only the facts that make its product look good while hiding the rest.
comprehension.explanation: The text explains that propaganda hides one side to make a product look better.

comprehension.question: Where and when is the story set? Describe the place in your own words.
comprehension.correctAnswer: It is set in the year 2083, in the green hills of what had once been northern Uganda, in a multicultural research village beside a protected grove.
comprehension.explanation: The opening paragraph gives the year, place and the village beside the grove.

comprehension.question: What does the grove's name, 'Nguvu Wa Asili', mean, and what is it?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It means 'Power of Nature', and it is the protected forest grove that the village cares for.
comprehension.explanation: The text translates the name and describes the grove the villagers protect.

comprehension.question: What two possible causes does Doctor Alina suggest for the forest drying out?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Radiation leaking from a forgotten machine buried during the old wars, or a bacterial plague.
comprehension.explanation: Doctor Alina names these two possible causes when Amal asks what is wrong.

comprehension.question: What does Amal create to help people care about the forest?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Posters, a display, a written report and a painted model of the forest's root system.
comprehension.explanation: Part 2 describes the posters, display, report and root-system model Amal makes.

comprehension.question: What decision does the council make at the end of part 2?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It agrees to ban further clearing near the grove and funds clean-up crews and radiation containment.
comprehension.explanation: The final paragraph states the council's ban and new funding.

comprehension.question: At the very end, Amal says the forest's recovery 'begins with belief'. What does she mean?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She means that protecting and restoring the forest starts when people believe change is possible and choose to act.
comprehension.explanation: Her closing words link belief and hope to the choice to take action.

grammar.title: What Is the First Conditional?
grammar.explanation: The First Conditional describes real, likely situations in the future and the result that will follow. We use it when there is a genuine chance that the condition will happen.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The First Conditional is a way of talking about things that are likely or possible in the future. We use it when we believe there is a real chance that something will happen, and we want to describe the result.
For example:
If you study hard, you will pass your test.
If it rains, we will cancel the picnic.
Every First Conditional sentence has two parts. The condition (the if-clause) describes what might happen. The result (the main clause) describes what will happen if the condition is met. It is called 'first' because it deals with real, likely possibilities. You will meet it in conversation, in news articles, in science writing and in stories, where it helps you talk about plans, warnings, advice and predictions.
grammar.commonMistake: Do not confuse the First Conditional with the Second Conditional. The First Conditional is for likely futures ('If it rains, we will stay in'); the Second is for imaginary ones ('If I had wings, I would fly').
grammar.memoryTip: Picture an 'If, then' bridge: the if-clause is one bank, the will-clause is the other, and the comma is the bridge that joins them.
grammar.practice: Part A: Underline the condition and circle the result in five First Conditional sentences from the reading passage. Part B: Explain in one sentence why each result is only 'likely', not certain.

grammar.title: How to Form the First Conditional
grammar.explanation: The First Conditional follows one clear pattern: If plus a subject and a present-simple verb, then a subject with will and the base form of the verb.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The First Conditional follows a clear, reliable pattern:
If + subject + present simple, subject + will + base verb.
Break it into steps. Start with the word If. Add a subject and a verb in the present simple. Put a comma after the if-clause. Then write the result with will (or will not) and the base form of the verb.
Examples:
If she practises every day, she will improve her speed.
If the team works together, they will win the tournament.
If we protect the forest, the ecosystem will survive.
Notice that the if-clause uses the present simple even though you are talking about the future. That surprises many learners, but it is the rule.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often add an extra 'to' after will, writing 'she will to improve'. After will, use the base verb with no 'to': 'she will improve'.
grammar.memoryTip: Chant the frame like a beat: 'If, present simple; will, base verb.' Say it aloud three times before you write.
grammar.practice: Part A: Complete ten sentences by putting the bracketed verbs into the correct forms. Part B: Write two First Conditional sentences of your own about training or healthy eating, then check the frame.

grammar.title: Swapping the Clauses and the Comma Rule
grammar.explanation: You can put the result first and the condition second. When the if-clause comes first you need a comma; when the result comes first you do not.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
You do not always have to begin with the if-clause. You can put the result clause first and the if-clause second, and the meaning stays exactly the same:
If you train hard, you will succeed. (comma after the if-clause)
You will succeed if you train hard. (no comma needed)
Both sentences mean the same thing, so changing the order simply makes your writing more varied and interesting. The comma is the key signal. When the sentence opens with the condition, mark the join with a comma. When it opens with the result, the reader does not need that comma, so leave it out.
grammar.commonMistake: A common slip is dropping the comma when the if-clause comes first, as in 'If it rains we will stay home.' Add the comma: 'If it rains, we will stay home.'
grammar.memoryTip: Remember: comma only when 'If' comes first. If the sentence starts with the result, no comma is needed.
grammar.practice: Part A: Rewrite five sentences so the result comes first, deleting the comma. Part B: Rewrite five more so the condition comes first, adding the comma.

grammar.title: Using 'Unless' Instead of 'If Not'
grammar.explanation: The word 'unless' means 'if not'. It lets you express a negative condition smoothly, but you must never add another negative after it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The word unless means 'if not'. Using it makes your conditional sentences sound natural and mature.
Compare:
If you do not drink enough water, you will feel tired.
Unless you drink enough water, you will feel tired.
Both mean the same thing. More examples:
Unless you practise, you will not improve.
The match will be cancelled unless the rain stops.
Because unless already carries the negative, you must not add 'not' or 'don't' after it, or you create a confusing double negative.
Incorrect: Unless you don't hurry, we will be late.
Correct: Unless you hurry, we will be late.
grammar.commonMistake: The biggest error with 'unless' is the double negative, such as 'Unless she doesn't study, she will fail.' Remove the second negative: 'Unless she studies, she will fail.'
grammar.memoryTip: Test any 'unless' sentence by swapping in 'if not'. If it still makes sense with no extra 'not', you have used it correctly.
grammar.practice: Part A: Rewrite six 'if not' sentences using 'unless'. Part B: Find and fix four sentences that contain a double negative after 'unless'.

grammar.title: Other Modal Verbs in the Result
grammar.explanation: The result clause usually uses 'will', but modal verbs like might, could, can, should and must change how certain, allowed or advised the result is.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Most First Conditional sentences use will in the result, but other modal verbs let you show different shades of meaning:
will shows a certain result: If she trains, she will improve.
might or may shows a less certain result: If it rains, we might stay indoors.
could shows a possible outcome: If she is late, she could miss the start.
can shows permission or ability: If you finish early, you can play outside.
should shows advice: If it snows, we should wear warm clothes.
must shows a strong obligation: If pollution increases, we must act.
Choosing the right modal makes your meaning far more precise.
grammar.commonMistake: Some learners keep the modal in the if-clause, writing 'If she will train, she will improve.' Keep the if-clause in the present simple; the modal belongs only in the result.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of a certainty dial: 'will' is turned up high, 'might' and 'could' sit in the middle, and 'should' gives friendly advice.
grammar.practice: Part A: Choose the best modal (might, could, should or must) to finish six results. Part B: Write one sentence each using 'might', 'should' and 'must' about health or the environment.

grammar.title: Editing First Conditional Mistakes
grammar.explanation: Skilled writers proofread for the four common First Conditional errors: 'will' in the if-clause, a missing comma, the wrong verb form after 'will', and double negatives with 'unless'.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Careful editing catches the four errors learners make most often.
1. 'Will' in the if-clause. Incorrect: If he will eat too much, he will get sick. Correct: If he eats too much, he will get sick.
2. A missing comma when the if-clause comes first. Incorrect: If it rains we will stay home. Correct: If it rains, we will stay home.
3. The wrong verb form after 'will'. Incorrect: The team will wins the match. Correct: The team will win the match.
4. A double negative after 'unless'. Incorrect: Unless you don't try, you will fail. Correct: Unless you try, you will fail.
Read each sentence slowly and check the if-clause, the comma and the verb after 'will' in turn.
grammar.commonMistake: The single most common error is putting 'will' in the if-clause. Whenever you see 'if ... will', pause and change the verb to the present simple.
grammar.memoryTip: Use the checklist 'if-clause, comma, base verb, no double negative' as a four-point proofreading sweep for every conditional you write.
grammar.practice: Part A: Correct eight sentences that each contain one of the four errors. Part B: Swap work with a partner and mark each other's First Conditional writing using the four-point checklist.

speaking.title: Speaking 1: Sports Interview Role-Play
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Work with a partner, or ask your AI tutor with an adult nearby, to role-play an interview. One of you is a journalist and the other is an athlete who has just won a big competition.
The journalist asks at least five questions, for example:
How did you first become interested in your sport?
What does your daily training routine look like?
What do you eat to stay healthy and strong?
How do you and your teammates cooperate during competitions?
If a young person wants to become an athlete, what advice would you give?
The athlete answers in full sentences, using unit vocabulary and at least two First Conditional sentences, such as, 'If I train every day, my fitness will improve.'
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Help me practise a sports interview role-play, then give me feedback on my clarity, my vocabulary and my use of complete First Conditional answers.

speaking.title: Speaking 2: Health Advice Presentation
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Prepare a short presentation of two to three minutes on one of these topics: why sleep matters for young athletes; how to eat a balanced diet; the benefits of team sport; or how to stay safe while exercising in hot weather.
Use at least three vocabulary words and at least three First Conditional sentences to give advice, such as, 'If you drink enough water, you will avoid feeling dizzy.'
When you present, speak clearly, make eye contact, and use your notes as a guide rather than reading them word for word. Structure your talk with a clear opening, two main points and a strong ending.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my two-minute health advice presentation and tell me how clearly I structured my main points and whether my First Conditional advice was accurate.

speaking.title: Speaking 3: Fact or Opinion Listening Game
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Your teacher or, with an adult present, your AI tutor will read out statements about sport, health and the environment. After each one, decide whether it is a fact that can be proven or an opinion that someone believes, and say your answer aloud with a reason.
Try these to begin: 'Running strengthens the heart.' 'Football is the best sport in the world.' 'Children need nine to eleven hours of sleep.' 'Swimming is more fun than running.'
Afterwards, discuss with a partner which signal words, such as 'best' or 'should', helped you spot the opinions.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Read me eight short statements about health, pause after each, and check whether I can correctly label it a fact or an opinion and explain how I decided.

speaking.title: Speaking 4: Sports Commentary Performance
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Using the sports commentary you wrote in the Writing Workshop, perform it aloud as if you were a live commentator on radio or television.
Speak with energy, letting your voice rise and fall to match the action. Pause for effect before big moments, and change your speed: faster for the exciting parts, slower for the tense build-up.
Record yourself, listen back, and ask, 'Does this sound exciting? Would a listener want to keep listening?' Then perform for a partner or family member and ask for feedback on your expression.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Listen to my recorded sports commentary and coach me on pace, energy and dramatic pauses so the performance sounds genuinely live and exciting.

speaking.title: Speaking 5: Science and Tradition Discussion
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
In a small group, discuss the story 'When the Leaves Stop Speaking'. Take turns to lead, and make sure everyone speaks.
Discuss these questions and give reasons: How do Amal and her grandfather show that science and tradition can work together? Do you agree that 'multicultural does not just mean people; it means ideas'? If the village had ignored Amal's evidence, what do you think would have happened?
Listen carefully, build on what others say, and show that you have considered a point of view that is different from your own.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Act as a discussion partner about the story's theme of science and tradition, then tell me whether I gave clear reasons and responded fairly to a different point of view.

speaking.title: Speaking 6: First Conditional Chain
speaking.instructionsAndModelLines:
Play a First Conditional chain with a partner. The result of one sentence becomes the condition for the next.
For example: 'If I eat a healthy breakfast, I will have more energy.' The next player continues, 'If I have more energy, I will train harder,' and so on.
Keep the chain going for at least six links about sport, health or protecting the environment. Speak in clear, complete sentences, and use the correct pattern: present simple in the if-clause and 'will' plus the base verb in the result.
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Play a spoken First Conditional chain with me for at least six turns, then point out any sentence where I slipped 'will' into the if-clause.

writing.title: Writing 1: Biography of a Sportsperson
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short biography of a sportsperson you admire. This can be a famous champion, someone from your community, or someone you invent. A biography is written in the third person, using 'he', 'she' or 'they', and it focuses on real facts and achievements.
Include the person's name, nationality and sport; when and where they grew up; how they began; their main achievements; at least three unit vocabulary words (underline them); and at least two First Conditional sentences about their future. End with a sentence explaining why this person inspires you.
writing.modelText: A strong response is organised into clear paragraphs in the third person, orders the events in time, weaves in precise unit vocabulary, and includes accurate First Conditional predictions about the athlete's future.
writing.successCriteria: I wrote in the third person; organised events in time order; included three unit words; used two First Conditional sentences; explained why the person inspires me; checked spelling and punctuation.
writing.support: Plan a timeline of facts before you write, then turn each stage of the person's life into its own paragraph.
writing.extension: Add a short quotation or a vivid detail, and vary your sentence openings so the biography reads smoothly from start to finish.

writing.title: Writing 2: Sports Commentary
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short sports commentary describing an exciting moment in a game or race of your choice. Commentators use short, energetic sentences and the present tense to make listeners feel as if they are watching live.
Include short, exciting sentences; present-tense verbs such as 'She runs! She shoots!'; at least two unit vocabulary words; at least one First Conditional sentence, such as, 'If she beats the defender, she will score'; and descriptive adjectives and adverbs to paint the picture.
writing.modelText: A strong commentary uses the present tense, short punchy sentences and vivid description to build excitement, and drops in at least one clear First Conditional prediction at a tense moment.
writing.successCriteria: I used the present tense throughout; wrote short, energetic sentences; included two unit words; used one First Conditional prediction; added vivid adjectives and adverbs; read it aloud to check the excitement.
writing.support: List five action verbs and five vivid adjectives before you begin, then build your commentary around them.
writing.extension: Add a dramatic pause with a dash, and finish on a surprising or triumphant final line that a listener will remember.

writing.title: Writing 3: Amal's Diary Entry
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Imagine you are Amal from 'When the Leaves Stop Speaking'. Write a diary entry about the day you gave your presentation at the youth assembly. Write in the first person, using 'I', 'my' and 'we', and describe both what happened and how you felt.
Include at least three unit vocabulary words and at least two First Conditional sentences about the forest's future, such as, 'If we act now, we will save the grove.'
writing.modelText: A strong diary entry uses the first person, records the events of the assembly in order, describes Amal's feelings honestly, and includes accurate First Conditional hopes for the forest.
writing.successCriteria: I wrote in the first person; described the assembly in order; showed how Amal felt; included three unit words; used two First Conditional sentences; checked my punctuation and spelling.
writing.support: Reread part 2 of the story first, then jot down three things that happened and three feelings before you write.
writing.extension: Show Amal's change of mood across the entry, moving from nervousness to hope, and use the vocabulary precisely.

writing.title: Writing 4: Letter to the Council
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Imagine you visited Amal's display. Write a letter to the mayor and council explaining why the forest should be protected. Set your letter out properly, with a greeting, clear paragraphs and a sign-off.
Persuade the reader using reasons and evidence from the story, at least three unit vocabulary words, and at least two First Conditional sentences, such as, 'If the council bans clearing, the ecosystem will recover.'
writing.modelText: A strong letter is set out correctly, states its purpose in the opening paragraph, builds a clear argument with reasons and evidence, and uses First Conditional sentences to show what will follow from the council's choices.
writing.expectedLength: Four organised paragraphs in a proper letter layout
writing.successCriteria: I used a greeting and sign-off; stated my purpose clearly; gave reasons and evidence; included three unit words; used two First Conditional sentences; organised my ideas into paragraphs.
writing.support: Plan your three strongest reasons first, then give each reason its own paragraph with evidence from the story.
writing.extension: Order your reasons from strong to strongest, and finish with a confident call to action for the council.

writing.title: Writing 5: Fact and Opinion Article
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write a short, balanced article about a health topic, such as sleep, healthy eating or team sport. Your job is to help readers tell facts from opinions.
Include at least three clear facts and at least two clearly signalled opinions; explain how a reader can tell the difference; use at least three unit vocabulary words; and include at least one First Conditional sentence, such as, 'If you check the evidence, you will spot the opinions.'
writing.modelText: A strong article separates proven facts from signalled opinions, explains how the reader can tell them apart, and stays balanced instead of pushing a single view.
writing.sentenceStarter: There are two kinds of statement in health writing:
writing.expectedLength: Four organised paragraphs with clear topic sentences
writing.successCriteria: I included three facts and two opinions; showed how to tell them apart; stayed balanced; used three unit words; included a First Conditional sentence; organised ideas into paragraphs.
writing.support: Sort your ideas into two columns, facts and opinions, before you write, then explain the difference in your own words.
writing.extension: Add a sentence about how advertisements can use propaganda, and show the reader how to check a claim for themselves.

writing.title: Writing 6: Environmental Poster and Explanation
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Design a poster and write an explanation that encourages people to protect the environment in your own community. First, invent a bold poster title, like Amal's, 'If the leaves stop speaking, who will listen?'
Then write an explanation of your poster. Use at least three First Conditional sentences to show what will happen if people do, or do not, act, and include at least three unit vocabulary words. Describe what your poster shows and why it will make people care.
writing.modelText: A strong response pairs a bold, memorable poster title with an explanation that uses several accurate First Conditional sentences to show cause and effect, and stays focused on a real local issue.
writing.expectedLength: Three organised paragraphs explaining the poster
writing.successCriteria: I invented a bold title; described what the poster shows; used three First Conditional sentences; included three unit words; focused on a real local issue; checked my spelling and punctuation.
writing.support: Choose one local issue you truly care about, then design your title and three First Conditional messages around it.
writing.extension: Explain how images and words work together on your poster, and end with a hopeful call to action for your community.

activities.title: Activities 1: Complete the First Conditional
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Fill in each blank using the correct form of the verb in brackets. Write the whole sentence.
1. If it (rain) tomorrow, we (cancel) the match.
2. If she (practise) her speech, she (succeed) in the presentation.
3. If we (plant) more trees, the air (become) cleaner.
4. If you (not eat) breakfast, you (feel) tired at school.
5. If the forest (continue) to deteriorate, the ecosystem (collapse).
6. If pollution (increase), the ozone layer (deteriorate).
activities.answerSummary: Model answers are provided for the teacher in the answer key.

activities.title: Activities 2: Rewrite Using 'Unless'
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Rewrite each sentence using 'unless' instead of 'if not', keeping the meaning the same.
1. If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
2. If the players do not cooperate, they will lose the match.
3. If she does not drink enough water, she will feel dizzy.
4. If we do not protect the forest, the ecosystem will collapse.
5. If they do not train every day, they will not win the tournament.
activities.answerSummary: Model answers are provided for the teacher in the answer key.

activities.title: Activities 3: Correct the Mistakes
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Each sentence contains one First Conditional mistake. Rewrite it correctly.
1. If he will study hard, he will pass the test.
2. If it rains we will cancel the picnic.
3. Unless you don't try, you will never succeed.
4. If she will eat healthy food, she will feel better.
5. The team will wins if they practise every day.
activities.answerSummary: Model answers are provided for the teacher in the answer key.

activities.title: Activities 4: Match the Halves
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Match each condition on the left with the result that fits best on the right. Write the pairs.
Conditions: 1. If you read every day, 2. If the weather is sunny, 3. If she eats a balanced diet, 4. If the players argue, 5. If we recycle more,
Results: a) she will be healthy and strong. b) we will help protect the environment. c) your English will improve. d) we will play outside. e) they will lose the match.
activities.answerSummary: Model answers are provided for the teacher in the answer key.

activities.title: Activities 5: Vocabulary Odd One Out
activities.instructionsAndItems:
In each group, circle the word that does not belong and write one sentence explaining why.
1. bacteria, mollusk, ozone, ecosystem (which one is not living or a system of living things?)
2. sculpture, architecture, texture, text (which one is not about art, buildings or design?)
3. radioactive, renewable, translucent, efficient (which one describes something dangerous?)
4. propaganda, sedition, agency, imagination (which two have negative meanings, and which is the odd one out?)

activities.title: Activities 6: Vocabulary Fill in the Blanks

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: Which word means 'to slowly become worse in quality'?
quizzes.explanation: 'Deteriorate' means to decline or grow worse; the others describe repair, reuse or working well.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: What does the word 'ecosystem' mean?
quizzes.options: A huge explosion when a star dies | A three-dimensional artwork made from stone or clay | A community of living things that depend on each other | Energy that travels as heat or light
quizzes.correctAnswer: A community of living things that depend on each other
quizzes.explanation: An ecosystem is a web of living things and their surroundings; the distractors define supernova, sculpture and radiation.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: Which sentence is a correct First Conditional?
quizzes.options: If it rains, we will cancel the match. | If it will rain, we will cancel the match. | If it rains, we cancelled the match. | If it rained, we will cancel the match.
quizzes.correctAnswer: If it rains, we will cancel the match.
quizzes.explanation: The if-clause needs the present simple and the result needs 'will' plus the base verb; the others break that pattern.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: In the First Conditional, which tense belongs in the if-clause?
quizzes.options: The future with 'will' | The past simple | The present continuous | The present simple
quizzes.explanation: Even though we mean the future, the if-clause uses the present simple, as in 'If she trains...'.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: Which word means the same as 'if not'?
quizzes.explanation: 'Unless' carries the meaning 'if not', so it replaces a negative if-clause.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: What does the word 'renewable' describe?
quizzes.options: Something dangerous that gives off energy | Something that spreads fear and lies | Something that can be replaced or used again | Something you cannot see through at all
quizzes.correctAnswer: Something that can be replaced or used again
quizzes.explanation: Renewable resources, like sun and wind, can be used again; the distractors describe radioactive, propaganda and opaque things.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: Choose the correct rewrite of 'Unless you don't hurry, we will be late.'
quizzes.options: Unless you hurry, we will be late. | Unless you don't hurry, we will be late. | If you don't hurry, we won't be late. | Unless you will hurry, we will be late.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Unless you hurry, we will be late.
quizzes.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding another negative or 'will' after it is wrong.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: What does the word 'transpiration' mean?
quizzes.options: The death of a large, exploding star | The way plants release water through their leaves | A serious disease that spreads quickly and makes people ill | The feeling of a rough or smooth surface
quizzes.correctAnswer: The way plants release water through their leaves
quizzes.explanation: Transpiration is how plants lose water through their leaves; the distractors define supernova, plague and texture.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: Which sentence uses a modal verb to give advice in the First Conditional?
quizzes.options: If it snows, we will stay home. | If it snows, we might stay home. | If it snows, we should wear warm clothes. | If it snows, we can stay home.
quizzes.correctAnswer: If it snows, we should wear warm clothes.
quizzes.explanation: 'Should' gives advice, while 'will', 'might' and 'can' show certainty, possibility and permission.

quizzes.quizTitle: Sports, Health and the Environment checkpoint
quizzes.question: Which of these statements is an opinion, not a fact?
quizzes.options: The body loses water through sweat during exercise. | Children need about nine to eleven hours of sleep. | Bacteria are too small to see without a microscope. | Football is the best sport in the whole world.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Football is the best sport in the whole world.
quizzes.explanation: 'Best' signals a personal view; the other three statements can be checked and proven.

liveSessions.title: Sports and Health: Launch, vocabulary and learning goals
liveSessions.beforeSession: Skim the unit overview and Vocabulary Group 1.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min welcome and goal-setting; 10 min teacher models six key words; 15 min learners build sentences in pairs; 10 min quick vocabulary game; 5 min feedback and next step.
liveSessions.afterSession: Choose five words you found hardest and write a sentence for each.

liveSessions.title: Sports and Health: Reading the science of sport
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read 'Training Champions' once and highlight any unknown words.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min retrieval of vocabulary; 10 min shared reading of the information text; 15 min comprehension in pairs with text evidence; 10 min fact-and-opinion hunt; 5 min review.
liveSessions.afterSession: Answer two comprehension questions in full sentences with quoted evidence.

liveSessions.title: Sports and Health: First Conditional in depth
liveSessions.beforeSession: Reread the grammar guide sections on forming the First Conditional.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min warm-up sentences; 10 min teacher models the pattern and the comma rule; 15 min guided practice with 'unless' and modals; 10 min partner editing; 5 min feedback.
liveSessions.afterSession: Write four First Conditional sentences, including one with 'unless'.

liveSessions.title: Sports and Health: Exploring the story
liveSessions.beforeSession: Read parts 1 and 2 of 'When the Leaves Stop Speaking'.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min recap of the plot; 10 min close reading of a key scene; 15 min group discussion of science and tradition; 10 min prediction with evidence; 5 min share-back.
liveSessions.afterSession: Write a short prediction about the forest, using evidence from two points in the story.

liveSessions.title: Sports and Health: Writing workshop: biography and commentary
liveSessions.beforeSession: Draft either the biography or the sports commentary before the session.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min model-text analysis; 10 min planning; 20 min guided drafting and paragraphing; 10 min peer feedback against the rubric.
liveSessions.afterSession: Revise one paragraph using the writing rubric and a partner's feedback.

liveSessions.title: Sports and Health: Speaking, presenting and review
liveSessions.beforeSession: Prepare your health advice presentation or sports commentary to perform.
liveSessions.agenda: 5 min speaking warm-up; 15 min performances and peer feedback; 10 min First Conditional chain game; 10 min unit review; 5 min self-assessment and goal-setting.
liveSessions.afterSession: Record your performance and note one strength and one target for next time.

teacherNotes.note: Model new language aloud, check meaning before independent work, and use mixed response modes. Give specific feedback on complete sentences, text evidence and precise vocabulary. Ensure a parent or another adult is present when learners use the AI tutor or record audio, and never leave a child alone with the device.

Encourage learners, with an adult nearby, to ask the AI tutor for help. Useful prompts include: 'What does the word deteriorate mean?', 'Can you explain the First Conditional in a different way?', 'Can you interview me about my favourite sport?', and 'Can you check my biography and tell me how to improve it?' Remind learners that the tutor supports their thinking rather than doing the work for them.
